title: The impact understanding of exosome therapy in COVID-19 and preparations for the future approaches in dealing with infec

predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The text states doses of "10 µg/ml, 20 µg/ml, 40 µg/ml, and 60 µg/ml were evaluated" and then says "a dose of 40 µg/mL (the highest dose) was selected as the optimal dose". 40 µg/mL is not the highest dose tested (60 µg/mL is), so the parenthetical justification contradicts the stated dose range. In addition, choosing a dose on the basis of viability differences that were explicitly "not statistically significant" leaves the dose selection unjustified.

predicted_errors.error_location: Abstract ("five COVID-19 patients in the intensive care unit, who were subjected to both inactivated SARS-CoV-2 and exosome therapy")
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The abstract describes patients as having been "subjected to ... exosome therapy", implying in vivo treatment of ICU patients. The Methods/Results make clear that only isolated PBMCs were exposed in vitro to inactivated virus and exosomes; no patient received exosome therapy. This misrepresents the experimental design.

predicted_errors.error_location: Abstract, final sentences ("exosome administration can effectively mitigate the hyperinflammation induced by COVID-19... underscore the potential safety and efficacy of exosomes as a therapeutic strategy")
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: No safety endpoint (toxicity, in vivo tolerability, clinical outcome) was assessed; the study is an in vitro PBMC cytokine assay in 5 patients and 5 controls. Claims of "safety and efficacy" and of effective mitigation of clinical hyperinflammation are unsupported by the reported evidence.

predicted_errors.error_location: Abstract ("when both groups were exposed to exosomes, there was a marked reduction in the levels of pro-inflammatory cytokines") vs Table 5
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: Table 5 shows that in healthy controls under the negative-control (unstimulated) condition exosomes produced no reduction: IL-6 median rose 2.041 → 2.998 (Z = 0.000, p = 1.000), IL-17 remained 0.000 → 0.000 (p = 1.000), and IFN-γ rose 0.000 → 2.665 with a reported significant p = 0.043. Thus exosomes did not reduce cytokines in "both groups" across conditions; in one case they significantly increased IFN-γ, contradicting the abstract's blanket claim.

predicted_errors.error_location: Table 5 and associated Results text (Wilcoxon Signed Ranks, n = 5)
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: All Wilcoxon comparisons report Z = ±2.023 with p = 0.043. Z = 2.023 is the normal (asymptotic) approximation obtained when all 5 pairs change in the same direction (T+ = 15, mean 7.5, SD 3.708). With only 5 pairs the exact two-tailed Wilcoxon p is 0.0625, i.e. non-significant at α = 0.05; the asymptotic approximation is invalid at this sample size. The claimed significance of exosome-induced reductions therefore rests on an inappropriate test statistic.

Footnotes c and d are given identical definitions ("Based on positive ranks"), making the superscripts uninterpretable. Moreover, rows with Z = 0.000 and p = 1.000 (healthy IL-6 and healthy IL-17 negative control) are labelled as based on positive ranks, which is inconsistent with a zero test statistic (which corresponds to footnote a, equal positive and negative rank sums, or to all-tied pairs).

predicted_errors.error_location: Results, flow cytometry paragraph ("These findings align with the criteria set by the International Society for Cellular Therapy for the definition of MSCs")
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The ISCT minimal criteria require positivity for CD73, CD90 and CD105 and negativity for CD45, CD34, CD14/CD11b, CD79a/CD19 and HLA-DR. The study tested only CD44 and CD90 (positive) and CD34/CD45 (negative); CD44 is not an ISCT criterion and CD73/CD105/HLA-DR were not assessed, so the data cannot be said to satisfy the ISCT definition.

The text asserts that identification requires "Detection of proteins enriched in exosomes, such as CD9, Tsg101, and Alix, and the absence of ... calnexin", but only CD9 detection and calnexin absence are actually reported; Tsg101, Alix, CD63 and CD81 were never shown. The conclusion that "the exosome-enriched pellet is indeed exosomes and not contaminating vesicles" overstates the presented characterization data.

predicted_errors.error_location: Introduction ("This miRNA acts as a silencing complex and alters the expression of cellular receptors through epigenetic modifications. This process inhibits various RNA viruses, including coronavirus, influenza, and hepatitis C, from invading the body")
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: miRNAs are loaded into the RNA-induced silencing complex (RISC); they are not themselves a "silencing complex", and the sweeping claim that this mechanism blocks coronavirus, influenza and HCV entry "into the body" is a mechanistic overstatement not supported by the cited literature.

predicted_errors.error_location: Discussion ("a retrospective observational study ... if the serum level of IL-6 exceeded 30 pg/mL, it was a predictor of the need for invasive mechanical ventilation")
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The commonly cited retrospective observational data on IL-6 predicting the need for mechanical ventilation in COVID-19 used a threshold of ~80 pg/mL (Herold et al.), not 30 pg/mL; the numerical cut-off attributed to the cited source appears misreported.
